raw_comment:
Watch out, Football Fans!

	This graph showcases a heavy left-skewed bimodal distribution between the percentage of football players diagnosed with chronic traumatic encephalopathy and the severity of injuries experienced within their respective football careers. There is an increased risk of chronic traumatic encephalopathy becoming more severe and even fatal as head injuries increase due to progressive disease symptoms.
	The graph showcases that football players are significantly more likely to develop chronic traumatic encephalopathy at more severe stages based on an increased cumulative injury force. With only 1696 football players in the NFL and this study utilizing 631 players, we know there is no sample size or speculation issue. 
	I wonder why the graph showcases around 35% of players with no chronic traumatic encephalopathy near the right end of the chart. It is an exact outlier compared to the rest of the data and completely ignores the established increasing trend. 
	Considering that my neighborhood is extremely close-knit and full of children who play basketball professionally, looking into the long-term effects of drastic injuries during the sport should be considered.

raw_comment:
This graph shows the cumulative force of head hits for 631 former football players and how that affected their  CTE. From this graph, I observe that more cumulative force usually creates greater head trauma, and less curative force results in less head trauma. CTE or chronic traumatic encephalopathy is associated with repeated blows to the head. Therefore it can be assumed that the more traumatic these hits are the more damage they will cause. I wonder if there is a direct correlation between the severity of the disease in the symptoms of memory loss, depression, aggressive behavior, and, sometimes, suicidal thoughts. This graph further demonstrates how unpredictable CTE can be at times. For example, if someone is hit with middle-level cumulative force they could have anywhere from no CTE at all to extremely severe stage 4 CTE. This could be a seriously life-changing difference for someone. However, there is a clear trend within the graph that directly relates more force with a greater CTE and less force with minor or no CTE. I really hope that this graph reaches the right audience and spreads awareness of contact sports such as football and boxing where head injuries are common. I also hope that this leaves an impact on people so much so that there become more regulations and/or head protective gear in these sports to try and prevent severe CTE for players, especially teens who will suffer the long-term effects.
“Watch Out Head Trauma Coming Your Way!”

I wonder about the presence of a segment of this graph where there is a high cumulative force but an abnormally lower percentage of players who have experienced CTE. I wonder if there are factors beyond cumulative force that also influence CTE onset such as genetics, individual resilience, or protective equipment that may influence CTE susceptibility.

As a high school student in New Jersey and given the prevalence of football culture within the northeast region of the United States, it is important to stay informed and up to date with these statistics because it can empower athletes, parents, coaches, and communities to make informed decisions regarding participation in the sport and advocate for safety measures.

I notice that in the graph, more cumulative force creates more stage 4 head traumas. As you go towards the right of the graph we start to see more Stage 3s and 4s as the cumulative force increases. raw_comment:
This graph depicts how head injuries have gravely impacted football players, specifically regarding chronic traumatic encephalopathy. Chronic traumatic encephalopathy, C.T.E. for short, a brain disease that can result from repeated trauma to the head, is currently both incurable and fatal. According to this graph, the more head trauma a football player experiences, the more likely they are to suffer from C.T.E. While C.T.E. can cause illnesses such as dementia, it has also been deteriorating mental health. Former players, Junior Seau, Philip Adams, and Dave Duerson, all diagnosed with severe depression from C.T.E., took their own lives. Aaron Hernandez and Jovan Belcher, both players suffering from C.T.E., were described as growing violent before commiting murder. I wonder why C.T.E., being such a pressing issue, is it not being discussed and researched more. Though this graph correlates brain injuries in football to chronic traumatic encephalopathy, this disease can be brought about by any high-contact sport. In my community, most people play or have played an intensive sport where concussions are prevalent. I have witnessed athletes be rushed to the hospital after serious head blows in sports ranging from soccer to cheerleading. As athletes in all sports continue to push the limits harder each year, will I have to worry about my teenage friends developing a life-threatening brain disease?

“What Is More Important: Pigskin or Your Life?”

raw_comment:
1. The first few things I notice are the main colors and how they increase with more hard hitting, but also the blank spot in the red. I find this anomaly extremely confusing and conclude it to be basic luck by the players that have suffered many head injuries, yet not end up with CTE. It does show that the people who have hit their head with the most cumulative force are always getting the worst cases of CTE and the people who get hit with the least cumulative force don’t get the worst type of CTE and over 50% don’t even get CTE at all.
2. The anomaly part of the graph where there is a section of people getting hit with more cumulative force, yet don’t get CTE is the part that interests me the most. This seems to be one of those weird things that happens where someone smokes and drinks their entire life and ends up living till their 90’s, something that just can happen by some sort of miracle. I think that this part of the graph just goes to show the weird possibilities human bodies can accomplish. 
3. This affects my community because football is played by people our age, meaning that people that haven’t even gotten to college could be getting CTE. I find that this is very dangerous and I feel that we should be finding a way to minimize injury in this sport until it dwindles down once people realize how weird it is to watch people just hit each other for a job. 
4. Catchy Title: CTE–Is It Really Worth It?

Over 1/3 of the players with the less forceful head hits still developed C.T.E. As I look toward the middle of the x-axis, the numbers of players with C.T.E. nearly triple. This disease seems almost inevitable for football players experiencing repetitive head trauma (which occurs often in the sport). I wonder what percentage of former NFL players have C.T.E., I think it is worthwhile to do a similar study with a much larger population in order to better grasp the amount of players C.T.E. affects/affected. If the number is concerning, more awareness could be brought to this disease and preventative measures could be taken. This relates to me and my community because I watch football very often in the fall and winter. I see players experience head hits that could possibly lead to C.T.E. later down the line. Knowing the true scale and implications of this disease makes me not want to watch football as it lends itself to traumatic head injuries and I do not want to support something that is causing so much widespread harm. I hope that others in my community would feel similarly if they knew more about C.T.E., and I am sure that many parents would discourage their children from participating in football.

raw_comment: I noticed that in the graph, the more the cumulative force of blows to the head during football, the higher the chance there is of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or C.T.E., a degenerative brain disease caused by a continuous amount of trauma induced to the head, which in this graph is displayed by sports accidents. Football, I’ve learned, is a very high-impact sport with great risk and plenty of injuries. Being a contact sport, it comes with the probability of sustaining dangerous injuries- head injuries. I wonder why some people tend to continue playing that specific sport after such injuries are induced, but I can understand that as a fellow athlete, it is difficult to walk away from your sport when you need to or have to due to injury. I have seen many football-related injuries in my years of high school or heard about certain severities of ones in the past, and have come to an understanding that football is more dangerous than I had suspected. I am not someone who enjoys football or watching sports in general, and I only run cross country and track, so mine aren’t contact sports at all (unless you count the occasional shove at the starting line). A good headline for this substantial and informative graph on head injuries in football would be “The Greater The Force, The Worse The Risk.” We should probably have more prevention of this disease and other high-impact injury protection protocols in this sport.

raw_comment: Football is a relatively dangerous sport, given how many players suffer from head injuries on average. A C.T.E., or Chronic traumatic encephalopathy, is a traumatic brain injury like a concussion. Football encourages players to tackle other players with extreme force to knock them down or remove obstacles. There is little control over how a person falls once they are hit, but how they are hit absolutely determines how badly they are injured. 100% of players who were hit with extreme force got a stage 4 C.T.E. upon impact on the ground. I notice how night numbers of players have received severe head trauma from the sport, but there is little education on how to prevent those injuries. Being hit with extreme force will lead to injury, but in the heat of the game, players are not actively thinking about injury prevention, only winning. I wonder why there is not more of an emphasis on safety in football. While players do wear padding, they are still praised for hard hits and tackles are a main part of the entertainment in TV coverage. It is upsetting to see how dangerous it is because of how popular the sport is for Americans both play and watch. With events like the Super Bowl, it is easy to forget how dangerous the game is for the players. We encourage good tackles and wild plays, but in reality, the safety of the players should be the most important part. The graph is showing the “Unmentioned dangers of Football” by exhibiting statistics of real injuries.

raw_comment:
1. The graph illustrates head collisions with either more or less force. You can tell that with more cumulative force the 60% of the players will suffer between Stage 3-4 C.T.E.. You can also see that out of the 631 former footballers majority will receive at least a stage of C.T.E..   This is depressing to see, the odds of getting C.T.E. is more likely to happen if you do ever end up playing. 

2. This makes me wonder what more protection will organizations like the NFL put on players to make it safer to play. Although there are already helmets and pads to take the impact they are not fully efficient. In the future will helmets be sustainable and renewable to be efficient enough to take hits. If not more inventions should be thought of to remove the risk of receiving C.T.E..

3. At our middle school the motivational speaker Eric Legrand payed a visit talking about his situation. I remember how he explained he hit his head on the ground while playing football causing him to be paralyzed from the neck down. He began receiving care and rehabilitation which nursed him back to health. He left the lesson that since he never gave up neither should we.

4. How do we ensure the safety of football players? Does protection stop at helmets?
